description: FinRisk knowledge base v1. General interpretation principles for financial ratios. Contains NO industry benchmarks or numeric thresholds. Add cited references (textbook, accounting standard, regulator guidance) in the 'source' field before final submission.

entries.title: Current ratio below 1.0
entries.content: A current ratio below 1.0 means reported current liabilities exceed reported current assets. Taken alone this indicates that short-term obligations are not fully covered by short-term assets. It must be interpreted together with operating cash flow and the speed at which inventory and receivables convert to cash, because companies with strong recurring operating cash generation can meet obligations from cash flow rather than from the asset balance.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Quick ratio and cash ratio
entries.content: The quick ratio excludes inventory and the cash ratio uses only cash and short-term investments. They are stricter liquidity tests than the current ratio. Low values indicate dependence on future cash inflows to settle current liabilities. Non-current marketable securities are excluded from these ratios even though they may be sellable, so the ratios can understate available liquidity for companies holding large long-term investment portfolios.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Operating cash flow relative to current liabilities
entries.content: Operating cash flow divided by current liabilities shows how much of the short-term obligations one year of operating cash generation could cover. It complements balance-sheet liquidity ratios, which are point-in-time measures, with a flow measure. A positive and substantial value can mitigate concerns raised by a low current ratio.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Debt-to-equity and low equity balances
entries.content: Debt-to-equity above 1.0 means reported debt exceeds shareholders' equity, indicating reliance on debt financing. The ratio is sensitive to the equity balance: share repurchases and dividends reduce equity, which can raise debt-to-equity even when debt has not increased. The ratio should therefore be read together with debt-to-assets, earnings and cash flow coverage rather than in isolation.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Debt ratio versus liabilities-to-assets
entries.content: The debt ratio counts only interest-bearing debt, while liabilities-to-assets includes all liabilities such as accounts payable, deferred revenue and other operating liabilities. A large gap between the two indicates that much of the liability base consists of non-debt operating liabilities, which carry different risk from borrowings.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Interest coverage unavailable
entries.content: Interest coverage measures how many times operating income covers interest expense. If interest expense is not separately disclosed, interest coverage cannot be calculated and must not be estimated. The assessment of debt-servicing capacity should then state this limitation explicitly.

entries.title: Margin analysis
entries.content: Gross, operating and net margins show how much of each unit of revenue remains after cost of sales, operating expenses, and all expenses including tax. Positive margins at all three levels indicate the company is profitable at each stage. Whether a margin is high or low can only be judged against industry peers or the company's own history; without such comparison data, only the direction and relative size of the margins can be described.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Return on equity inflated by low equity
entries.content: Return on equity uses shareholders' equity as the denominator. When equity is small relative to assets, for example after large share repurchases, ROE can be very high without reflecting unusually strong operating performance. A very high ROE should be cross-checked against return on assets and leverage before being treated as a sign of profitability.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Return on assets
entries.content: Return on assets relates net income to total assets and is less affected by financing structure than ROE. Using period-end assets instead of average assets is a simplification; when prior-year balances are available, average balances give a more accurate measure.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Turnover ratios
entries.content: Turnover ratios measure how quickly assets, inventory and receivables are converted into revenue or cash. Higher inventory and receivables turnover generally mean less cash is tied up in working capital, which supports liquidity. Appropriate turnover levels vary strongly by industry and business model, so without industry data only the relative magnitude can be described. Period-end balances are a simplification of average balances.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Negative financing cash flow
entries.content: A negative financing cash flow means more cash was paid to capital providers than was raised from them. Typical causes are debt repayment, dividends and share repurchases. It is not inherently a risk signal; it becomes a concern only if it is not funded by operating cash flow and erodes cash reserves.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Operating cash flow versus net income
entries.content: Operating cash flow that is positive and of similar size to net income indicates that reported earnings are largely backed by cash. Operating cash flow persistently and substantially below net income can indicate weaker earnings quality.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Net change in cash
entries.content: A small negative net change in cash, when operating cash flow is strongly positive, usually reflects capital allocation decisions such as distributions to shareholders or investment activity rather than operating weakness. The size of the change relative to the cash balance matters more than its sign.
entries.source: General financial statement analysis principle (add citation)

entries.title: Single-period analysis limitation
entries.content: An assessment based on one fiscal year cannot show trends. Ratios computed from a single period should be presented as a snapshot. Industry benchmarks and peer comparisons are required to classify a ratio as strong or weak in absolute terms; if they are not available, the assessment must say so rather than assume a benchmark.
